sermon.title: Deflective Defective Disciples Part 2
sermon.speaker: Pastor David G. Kincer
sermon.summary: In “Deflective Defective Disciples Part 2,” Pastor David G. Kincer continues the previous message by saying the Bible’s “I believe” statements are about believing Jesus is the Son of God and that God will do what he said. He argues from Acts and 1 Corinthians that Christians and ministers are meant to judge, reads Revelation 21:8 on who goes to the lake of fire, and criticizes ministers he says flatter people. He points to Jeremiah 3:15 as God’s solution and calls believers to virtue and to speak up.
sermon.transcript_source: This transcript comes from YouTube’s automatic English captions, which supply the timing and the words. Punctuation, casing, paragraphing and obvious caption errors were cleaned by hand; his wording was not rewritten. “[unclear]” marks a word or name that was not clear. Bracketed notes are added by the editor.

chunks.section_question: Do Christians need personal prophecy, and will good people go to heaven without Christ?
chunks.short_answer: Pastor Kincer lists prosperity, positive thinking, possibility, Purpose Driven and psychotherapy thinking, and adds personal prophecy thinking, which he says is a dime a dozen in many Spirit-filled circles. He says he does not need personal prophecy; he needs the Bible, the sure word of prophecy. He says the claim that atheists, humanists and anyone who is good can go to heaven is lying, and that the end result of Jesus’s faith is a disciple pursuing the divine nature and doing good works.
chunks.text:
Adultery, homosexuality, incest, intoxication. Okay, see, “my faith,” “I believe,” nothing’s wrong with it. Prosperity, positive thinking, possibility— you ever met these people that won’t say a negative thing? There: possibility thinking, prosperity thinking, Purpose Driven thinking, psychotherapy thinking, and one I didn’t have up there is this personal prophecy thinking. My gosh. And in a lot of Spirit-filled circles, you know, personal prophecy is just a dime a dozen. Just everybody’s giving out personal prophecies. Where is that in the Bible? They’re just flat out wrong. I don’t need no personal prophecy; I need the book. I need the Bible. Amen. It’s the sure word of prophecy, that’s what the Bible says.

Atheist and humanist and everybody’s got their own ideas. And in one of these they talked about atheists, and they said, yeah, everybody can go to heaven. And as Oprah put it, if you’re good— generosity, kindness and love— you can go to heaven no matter what. They’re just lying. Now, over here the end result is a Christian, a disciple of the divine nature. They’re pursuing the divine nature. Hallelujah, because that’s what this faith, Jesus’s faith, whole focus is on: you being a light to the world, living for him by doing good works.

chunks.section_question: Who goes to the lake of fire according to Revelation 21:8, and should preachers challenge sin?
chunks.short_answer: He reads Revelation 21:8 and says it plainly tells who is going to the lake of fire, including the unbelieving, abominable, murderers, sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters and all liars. He says homosexuals miss out on two counts, sexual immorality and abomination, and that you cannot change the Bible because you want to be nice to people. He says preachers are not challenging Christians living in sexual immorality, and that America and the homosexual need to hear it so he can get saved and change his ways.
chunks.text:
Now, Revelation 21:8: “The cowardly, the unbelieving, the abominable”— abomination means God hates it, all right— “murderers, sexually immoral, sorcerers,” which is witchcraft, “idolaters, and all liars shall have their part in the lake which burns with fire and brimstone, which is the second death.” And Joel Osteen doesn’t know, and T. D. Jakes doesn’t know, that these people are going to hell, and Rick Warren doesn’t know, and Oprah doesn’t know. It’s very plain in Revelation. This is just one scripture. He tells us plainly who’s going to the lake of fire, and homosexuals miss out on two counts: sexual immorality and abomination. It’s listed under both. Adultery, incest— these sins, will you burn for them? You can’t change the Bible because you want to be nice to people. Can I hear an amen?

And Christians are living in sexual immorality and doing all kinds of stupid things, and the preachers aren’t challenging them on Sunday to stop it, and everybody thinks they’re okay. Folks, you can’t change this. Idolatry is an abomination. Idolatry is listed twice up there, under abominations and under idolatry. Are you with me? And all liars: these guys are lying. How many liars go to hell? All of them. Now, folks, this is flagrant lying just so they can get crowds and money. They like the money, man. They live in million-dollar mansions and they drive big cars, and they got all these people coming wanting to hear their flattering messages. And America needs to hear that that’s wrong, and the Christians need to hear, the homosexual needs to hear that he’s wrong, so that he can get saved and change his ways. Can I hear an amen?

chunks.section_question: What does “I believe” mean in the Bible?
chunks.short_answer: He says “I believe” is used four times in the passages he reads and every time it means believing that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, the only begotten Son of God, or believing that God will do what he said he would do. He reads the statements in John 11, John 9, Acts 8 and Acts 27, and says that is what “I believe” should say, not that any sin is fine and you can still go to heaven.
chunks.text:
But so, the adulterers. John 11:27, the statement of “I believe”: “I believe you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is to come into the world.” Okay. “I believe” is used four times, and every time it’s used this way. All right: I believe Jesus Christ is the Son of God, the only begotten Son of God. Lucifer is not a begotten Son of God. Lucifer was a created being. Jesus was birthed in the flesh by God. Amen.

John 9:35: “Do you believe on the Son of God?” Jesus asked the man. He said, “Who is he, Lord, that I might believe on him?” Jesus said, “You have seen him, and it is he that talks with you.” I’m him, Jesus said. The man quickly says, “I believe.” I believe what? That you are the Son of God, that Jesus is the Son of God. How many believe that Jesus is the only begotten Son of God? Yeah. See, that’s what “I believe” should say: not “I believe homos can go to heaven,” and, “Oh, you know, I can get intoxicated and still go to heaven,” and all the rest. No.

Acts 8:37: Philip said, “If you believe with all your heart, you may get baptized,” and the eunuch said, “I believe Jesus Christ is the Son of God.” He said it again. Paul, in Acts 27:25, on the island— or before he got to the island, on the boat: “Be of good cheer, I believe God.” What’s the statement? “I believe God that it shall be as it was told me.” Now, that sums it up: I believe that God will do what he said he would do. Amen. I can’t come up with my own little gizmo doctrines, my feel-good doctrines.

chunks.section_question: Does the Bible say we should not judge anyone?
chunks.short_answer: He says ministers are supposed to preach the Bible, and the Bible already judges, so telling people they are going to hell is telling them what the Bible said, not judging them himself. He compares it to a doctor who will not tell a patient with cancer he is going to die, and says Paul boldly told the Jews who rejected the word that they had judged themselves unworthy of eternal life.
chunks.text:
The Bible, in judging: you hear them all say they wouldn’t judge. You hear that? I’m not going to judge anybody. Well, no, all sinned. T. D. Jakes, all not going to judge: I’m not going to judge. Well, the Bible already judges it. And ministers are supposed to be preaching the Bible. See, I’m not judging people when I, you know, when I tell people you’re going to hell. I’m telling them what the Bible said. God’s judgment is you’re going to hell. And I told you people last year said nobody talks like that. I said, the Bible talks like that.

And can you imagine going in for cancer, and the doctors don’t want to make a judgment? They don’t want to tell you that you’re going to die, and they just say, oh, you’re just fine, you’re just fine, you’re not going to die, you don’t need treatment, you’re just— you don’t need any kind of treatment, you don’t need any kind of medicine or anything else, you know. And in the end you what? Die, when you could have got some treatment and lived. And these preachers don’t want to tell people they’re going to die. See, the lake of fire we read is the second death. You’re going to die for eternity.

The Jews opposed things spoken by Paul, in Acts 13:45. So Paul boldly said— Paul what? Boldly said. He didn’t sit there silently and, well, I’m not going to judge. Well, you know, I haven’t read into that, I don’t have knowledge. No, he boldly said, “It was necessary the word of God be spoken to you first, you Jews, but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, we’re going to the Gentiles.” See, they judged themselves. They made a decision themselves to miss out on eternal life.

chunks.section_question: Are Christians supposed to make judgments, according to 1 Corinthians 6 and Acts 15?
chunks.short_answer: He says 1 Corinthians 6 asks whether the saints will judge the world and angels, so they are not unworthy to judge the smallest matters of this life. He reads Acts 15:19, where the decision is to write to the Gentiles to abstain from idols, sexual immorality, things strangled and blood, and he says ministers should make that judgment today.
chunks.text:
1 Corinthians 6:2: “Do you not know that the saints would judge the world?” Whoo! Are you out there, church? “If the world will be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters?” You can’t make decisions on the least little thing! You got these homosexuals and these Oprah telling you that— “Judge not, lest you be not judged. For what judgment you judge you shall be judged.” Come on!

“Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more things that pertain to this life?” Are we supposed to make judgments concerning this life? Yeah. Are we to make judgment on the very smallest matters, whether we buy a car we can’t afford, or will we buy a car we can’t afford? Are we supposed to make judgments? Yeah. Good grief. Raise your child up in the way they should go, or raise them up the way Dr. Spock said they should go? We got to make— we’re to make judgment. They’re lying to you, people out there.

Acts 15:19: “I judge.” What did he say? “I judge.” [Editor’s note: in Acts 15:19 the speaker is James, not Paul.] Oh my gosh, [unclear] is going to fall off his chair. Oprah and T. D. Jakes and Warren, what’s this? What are they going to do with this scripture? Paul’s judging. He’s making a decision. What’s his decision? “That we should not trouble the Gentiles who are turning to God, but that we write to them to abstain from things polluted by idols, sexual immorality, things strangled, and from blood.” Sexual immorality: no homosexuality, no adultery, no incest, no sex with kids, all sex in the marriage. That’s it. And he made that judgment. Don’t you think ministers should be making that judgment today? Absolutely.

chunks.section_question: Why are so many Christians weak, and what should they do?
chunks.short_answer: He says God’s people are weak because they listen to weak preachers and do not have enough discipline to read the Bible themselves every day. He says Christians in trouble are non-readers who go to Bible studies mostly to associate with a group, and that they should get a connection with Jesus and his word, since we go to church to spiritualize, not socialize.
chunks.text: God’s people are wimps because they’re listening to wimpy ministers. That’s right. They’re weak because they listen to weak preachers, and they ain’t got enough discipline to get on their knees and open that Bible up themselves and read a proverb a day and read [unclear] a day and read the Bible every day. I guarantee you, Christians that are in trouble are non-readers, and they don’t go to Bible studies where they actually hear somebody expound and open up the scriptures to them. They go to Bible studies mostly to associate, you know, they’re associating with this group, they got a connection with the group. You better get a connection with Jesus and his word. Yeah, that’s worth a clap. We don’t go to church to socialize. These churches, America’s churches, have got it wrong. We go to church to spiritualize. We need to become better spiritual people. Hallelujah.

chunks.short_answer: He reads 1 Corinthians 5 and says Paul told the church not to keep company with the sexually immoral and others in the list, and that those inside the church are to be judged while God judges those outside. He says the man there was committing incest, and Paul passed a judgment to kick him out of the church.
chunks.text: 1 Corinthians 5:9: “I wrote to you not to keep company with sexually immoral brethren, or greedy people, extortioners”— and revilers, they that blast people with their mouth— “drunkard, or idolaters. Not to eat with such a person. What have I to do with judging outsiders? Do you not judge those who are inside?” Did you hear that? “But those outside God judges. For this reason, put away yourselves from that evil person.” This guy was committing incest. He was having sex with his father’s wife, and Paul passed a judgment to kick this guy out of the church, and he told the Corinthian church, you got to make decisions.

scriptures.text_nkjv: I wrote to you in my epistle not to keep company with sexually immoral people. Yet I certainly did not mean with the sexually immoral people of this world, or with the covetous, or extortioners, or idolaters, since then you would need to go out of the world. chunks.section_question: What does it mean to live for Christ instead of for yourself?
chunks.short_answer: He reads 2 Corinthians 5:14 and calls it basic kindergarten Christianity: if Christ died for you, you should live not for yourself but for him. He says selfishness is why churches have problems, and that following Jesus’s example means laying down our life, working, getting married, staying married and raising children right.
chunks.text:
2 Corinthians 5:14: “The love of Christ compels, because we judge this: if one died for all, then all died, and he died for all, that those who live should live no longer for themselves.” Good Lord, that’s so simple. That’s basic kindergarten Christianity: that if Christ died for you, you should be living not for yourself but for him who died for you and rose again. Can I hear an amen? I don’t have to live to please Rick Warren or T. D. Jakes or Joel Osteen. I’ve got to please Jesus Christ. Amen.

And let me tell you something, church: selfishness is why you got your problems. You’re only thinking about yourself and your feelings and what you want, and it creates problems. You just want your own way because you feel it’s right. Jesus, our example, laid down his life for us. If we’re going to follow his example, we’re going to what? Lay down our life. We’re not going to do what we want to do; we’re going to do what he wants us to do. Amen. We’re going to work, we’re going to get married, we’re going to stay married, we’re going to raise children, we’re going to raise them right. We judge this way. Are we to judge? Yes.

chunks.section_question: Should preaching and prophecy be tested against the Bible?
chunks.short_answer: He reads 1 Corinthians 14:29, let two or three prophets speak and let the others judge, and says he has a right to decide whether what ministers say is scripturally correct. He says personal prophecy has no one to verify it and that prophets should not be wrong, and that people must depend on the scriptures. He also says we are to judge ourselves, and that the Sermon on the Mount means start with yourself before helping a brother with a splinter.
chunks.text:
1 Corinthians 14:29: “Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others”— what? Judge. See, I have a right to take what Joel Osteen, Rick Warren, T. D. Jakes and Oprah and all these guys say. I have a right to make a decision if they’re scripturally correct. And I’m not out to lambaste the brethren or to divide the church. I am out to speak the truth so people can know the truth and the truth can set them free. Is that an amen?

I mean, it plainly says when somebody’s talking, there’s got to be somebody checking out whether they’re saying it right or not. Hallelujah. And that’s where personal prophecy goes right out the tube. There’s no one there to verify you’re speaking right. chunks.section_question: Why should Christians speak up instead of staying silent?
chunks.short_answer: He says people who come to church, never share Christ with anybody and go home are silent saints who have no effect in the kingdom. He says that when you really know something it is natural to talk about it, without pumping up courage, and that you should speak the truth and not argue, since if one person is silent the argument ends.
chunks.text:
You know, there’s people that come to church and they never share Christ with anybody. They have no effect and [unclear] in the kingdom at all. They just come, hear a sermon, go, oh wow, what a great sermon. Hallelujah. Do their little thing that they do in their church and then go home, and they’re silent saints. They are worthless. And I’m looking at some today. We got the internet; you can talk to anybody. I told you I went right to Utah, talked right to headquarters.

How you know it’s time to speak up, hallelujah: it’s natural. When you really experience something and you know something, it’s just natural to talk about it. It isn’t like you got to get the courage up and pump it up. It’s just natural. You know, when somebody’s into baseball, it’s natural that they talk about baseball, right? People that are into God and truth, it’s just natural to speak truth, and you don’t have to argue about it. Just speak it and shut up. The Bible says it takes two people to argue; if one is silent, the argument ends. If you read your Proverbs you would know, but most of you do not read your Proverbs every day, principles of life.

chunks.section_question: What responsibility do believers have to get this message out?
chunks.short_answer: He says to whom much is given much is required, so the church has a responsibility to get organized and tell everyone, believer and unbeliever alike, that Bible morality is part of getting into heaven. He says Bible morality, not psychotherapy and positive thinking, is what blesses a family and helps people in the church, and that it challenges immoral people to change.
chunks.text: They’re all going to the lake of fire, folks. Now, because we know that to whom much is given, much is required, we have a responsibility to get this word out. We have a responsibility, church, to get organized and get out this message to everyone, believer and unbeliever alike, that Bible morality is part of getting into heaven. Amen. And Bible morality is what blesses my family. That’s what’s going to encourage my children, being an example and teaching them and directing them that way. That’s what’s going to help my family. It isn’t psychotherapy and positive thinking. Bible morality is what’s going to help people in the church, and it’s going to challenge the unmoral people to change their way. And that’s what the basic gospel is all about.

faqs.answer: He says it is natural when you really experience something to talk about it, like someone into baseball talking about baseball. He says people into God and truth naturally speak truth, and you do not have to argue about it.

faqs.question: What does he say about avoiding heated arguments?
faqs.answer: He says you can say your statement and shut up, since it takes two people to argue and if one is silent the argument ends. He says there is no sense in harping on it again and again; just say it and go on and let God do the work.
